content: The effectiveness of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in reducing the progression from TB infection to active disease is estimated to range between 60% and 90%, with protection lasting for several years. However, despite its proven benefits, the global implementation of TPT has been slow, necessitating urgent measures to accelerate its programmatic uptake. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic poses significant challenges to TB prevention and care worldwide, including the rollout of TPT. Nevertheless, TB programs must continue to scale up their services and seek synergies with COVID-19 control measures. Individuals confined to their homes due to COVID-19 may face increased exposure to TB within their households, emphasizing the importance of contact investigation to address both conditions and expand TPT coverage among contacts. This call to action outlines key considerations for countries integrating TPT into their TB prevention strategies, in alignment with recent global guidelines. It primarily targets program managers and technical agencies, assisting them in revising strategies and preparing funding proposals. Strengthening contact investigation is highlighted as a critical activity, as it remains underdeveloped in many countries, with a substantial unmet need for TB preventive measures. This does not diminish the importance of ensuring adequate TPT coverage among people living with HIV (PLHIV) and other high-risk groups. TPT should be regarded as an essential component of a comprehensive TB strategy, particularly in the absence of a near-term immunizing vaccine. National TB strategic plans and funding proposals should include TPT activities with ambitious targets and appropriate budgets. Contact investigation is vital for identifying individuals exposed to active TB, who are at increased risk of infection and disease. The risk of TB disease can be as high as 5% or more among household contacts, especially children. PLHIV exposed to active TB are at an even higher risk of rapid progression to TB disease. Contact investigation aims to identify these individuals and assess their need for treatment for TB disease or TPT. These activities can halt the progression of infection and enable early treatment, reducing disease severity, mortality, and transmission. Contact investigation can also identify individuals exposed to drug-resistant TB, requiring tailored approaches to TPT and follow-up. In high HIV burden settings, TPT for contacts in HIV care can be integrated into differentiated HIV service delivery (DSD) models, which are being scaled up for antiretroviral (ARV) services and intensified TB case finding. However, TPT provision for PLHIV should not be delayed until DSD is fully established. Beyond households, contact investigation and active TB case finding are also crucial in congregate settings and healthcare facilities. These include individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplants, or those with silicosis, as well as prisoners, healthcare workers, migrants, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. Governments and donors must allocate sufficient funding and human resources to support effective household contact investigation and management. This includes recruiting adequate staff, mobilizing communities, providing transport support, ensuring access to diagnostics, supplying medications, supporting treatment adherence, modernizing record-keeping, and funding operational research to identify optimal care models for scaling up TPT activities. Testing for TB infection using tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) helps direct TPT to those who would benefit most, avoiding unnecessary treatment and associated harms. A positive test result may also motivate individuals to adhere to TPT. However, national programs currently face limited testing capacity. Quality-assured TST is in short supply, and IGRAs are more expensive and require blood samples to be processed in well-equipped laboratories. Addressing these infrastructural and supply barriers is desirable, with a long-term goal of building health system capacity for testing, including human resources, logistics, supply chains, and monitoring and evaluation. This will also facilitate the rapid rollout of new, improved point-of-care tests for TB infection in the future. In the short term, the unavailability of TST/IGRA should not hinder TPT provision to high-risk groups. For children under five years in contact with active TB and PLHIV, TB infection testing is not required due to the urgency of treating exposure in these populations. Excluding active TB disease before starting TPT is essential, and chest radiography can play a critical role in this process, increasing confidence in TPT. Counseling is another important component of person-centered care, helping individuals make informed decisions about TPT based on a clear understanding of its potential benefits and risks. Governments and donors should ensure the uninterrupted supply of TPT medicines and promote the transition to optimal TPT approaches for both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB. They should strive for person-centered approaches, upholding privacy and protection from stigma. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of TPT programs should focus on three key indicators: coverage of contact investigation, TPT initiation, and TPT completion. M&E activities should be integrated into existing national health management information systems. Governments and donors should promote the use of electronic data capture to generate strategic information and collect additional data useful for individual care, such as patient-level reporting on adverse events during treatment and corrective actions taken. The Ministry of Health should establish or strengthen a joint national coordinating body and/or technical expert working group to support the national scale-up of TPT in line with the latest global guidelines. This body should oversee governance, planning, coordination, and implementation of TPT services, as well as mobilize financial resources from governments and donors. It should also provide technical advice on scaling up TPT, review emerging evidence, update national policies and guidelines, and develop tools to address provider concerns and dispel myths about TPT. The joint national coordinating body should include representatives from relevant ministries, national TB and HIV programs, implementing partners, civil society, and at-risk populations. Regular meetings should be convened to address priority issues, with funding allocated for these activities. When preparing a budget for TPT programs, key cost determinants include the estimated burden of TB, investigation of target populations, human resources, TPT provision and follow-up, laboratory work, supervision, drug distribution, capacity building, demand creation, and M&E. Governments and donors should ensure adequate resources to support these activities and promote the use of electronic tools for data recording and reporting.
